text.en: A farmer in the plains sows in the monsoon, harvests in the autumn, sows again in winter and harvests in spring. An old verse says that a farmer who looks after his cattle, visits his fields daily, knows the seasons, is careful about seeds and is industrious is rewarded with harvests of all kinds. In this chapter we follow the story of farming in India, from ancient rice grains to drip irrigation.

Agriculture is the main livelihood of a large share of India's people. A little over 18 percent of the value of all goods and services produced in a year (the gross domestic product) came from agriculture and allied activities in 2022-23. Besides growing crops, some farmers practise pisciculture, fish rearing, or rear cocoons to get silk thread. Many farm tasks from sowing to harvesting and threshing are done by hand or with machines. Archaeologists have found rice grains in the Ganga Plain as early as the 7th or 8th millennium BCE. Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, fowl and other animals were domesticated from the pre-urban phase of the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation, about 3500 BCE.
India's varied geography and climate decide which crops grow where and when. Indian agriculture has three main cropping seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid. Kharif crops, such as rice, maize, cotton and sugarcane, are sown with the south-west monsoon in June or July and harvested in September to October. They depend on the timely arrival of the monsoon. The north-east monsoon prevails from October to December and helps farming in Tamil Nadu and nearby areas. Rabi crops, such as wheat, barley, mustard and gram, are sown in the cool season, in October or November, and harvested in March or April. Zaid crops, such as watermelon, cucumber and vegetables, are grown in the short summer season between rabi and kharif. This grouping helps governments and agencies plan what, when and how to grow different crops.
Soil is a complex living ecosystem with bacteria, fungi, earthworms and insects. Humus, the dark organic part of soil, makes it fertile. If the same crop is grown again and again, the soil loses nutrients. Farmers traditionally rotated crops so that there would be periodic harvests from the same field. Rain-fed agriculture depends entirely on rainfall. The history of irrigation in India is very long, with canals, tanks, wells and step wells. In some hill areas farmers use bamboo pipes to bring spring water to fields. Drip irrigation delivers water drop by drop to plant roots and wastes little. Sprinkler irrigation sprays water into the air which falls like rain. Seeds are the beginning of the crop. High-yielding, pest-resistant seeds are developed by scientific processes. Traditionally, farmers also coated seeds with beejamrit, a paste of cow dung, urine and other materials, a method promoted by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) today. Seeds are also kept in storehouses such as the kulagar.
The Green Revolution, in which M. S. Swaminathan played a leading role, used high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation to greatly increase food production. It made India self-sufficient in food, but heavy use of chemicals and water has hurt soil health and groundwater. Natural and organic farming is inspired by Indian Knowledge Systems and focuses on environment-friendly, long-lasting practices. Precise application of fertilisers uses them efficiently and keeps the soil healthy. Agriculture is not always enough to give farmers a decent quality of life, and farmers need fair prices and support. Rivers like the Ganga support farming for millions, so their pollution and drying would threaten agriculture and food production in the basin.

problem.en: Classify as kharif, rabi or zaid: wheat, rice, watermelon.

text.en: Rice needs monsoon water: kharif.
Wheat needs a cool season: rabi.
Watermelon is grown in the dry summer: zaid.

prompt.en: Explain how farmers can protect soil and save water.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking one crop all year is best.

points.en: India has three crop seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid.
Soil health and water use decide long-term farming.
Drip and sprinkler irrigation save water.
The Green Revolution raised food output; sustainable farming protects the land.
